nuclear_aggregation.name: Google–Kairos Power Master Plant Development Agreement
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Google and Kairos Power signed a Master Plant Development Agreement (Oct 2024) covering a fleet of advanced reactor plants totaling 500 MW by 2035, first unit by 2030. Kairos develops/constructs/operates each plant and sells power via individual PPAs under the master framework; the agreement includes milestone-based accountability rather than a single upfront price.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Signed Oct 14 2024; framed by Kairos/Google as 'the first corporate agreement for multiple deployments of a single advanced reactor design in the United States.' No unit operating yet as of this research; no public per-unit pricing schedule disclosed.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Not disclosed. CEO Mike Laufer says the fleet structure lets Kairos 'quickly advance down the learning curve as we drive toward cost and schedule certainty,' implying later units benefit from learning, but no rebate/discount mechanism for early Google commitments is public.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: Shows a single hyperscaler acting as its own multi-unit demand pool (a degenerate 'buyer's club of one') to unlock fleet-level learning-curve pricing — the mechanism a microreactor orderbook would need to replicate across many smaller buyers.

nuclear_aggregation.name: Amazon–X-energy 5 GW framework
nuclear_aggregation.category: nuclear demand aggregation / corporate offtake + equity
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Amazon's Climate Pledge Fund led a $500M equity round in X-energy (Oct 2024) alongside a framework to support >5 GW of Xe-100 projects across the US through 2039 — the largest commercial SMR deployment target announced to date. Separate site-specific deals were struck in parallel: a Carbon Free Development and Funding Agreement with Energy Northwest for 4 reactors (320 MWe, upsizable to 960 MWe), and a feasibility agreement with Dominion Energy (≥300 MW).
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: $500M raised for X-energy in 2024; X-energy later raised >$1B in its 2026 IPO. Amazon/X-energy describe a 'standardized deployment and financing model' to replicate across future utility partners, but no single binding 5 GW purchase order exists — it is a target plus staged site deals.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: Illustrates demand aggregation led by one large offtaker stitching together multiple site-level orders under one reactor design and one financing template — the 'buyers' consortium of convenience' pattern a microreactor platform could formalize contractually across many buyers instead of one.

nuclear_aggregation.name: Equinix–Radiant 20-unit Kaleidos preorder with deposits
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Equinix signed a preorder agreement and paid real cash deposits (not a letter of intent) for 20 Kaleidos microreactors (1 MW each, shipping-container form factor, 5-year no-refuel) from Radiant, announced Aug 14 2025. First Kaleidos Demonstration Unit tests at Idaho National Laboratory's DOME facility in 2026; initial customer deployments targeted 2028.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Described by Radiant as its largest deal to date and 'the largest deal to date for any mass-manufactured reactor.' No public per-unit price or price-decline schedule disclosed.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Not disclosed — no public information on whether Equinix's per-unit price is fixed, declining, or rebate-eligible as later buyers join Radiant's book.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: The most directly relevant existing microreactor precedent: a real-money 20-unit preorder is already below the ~30-50 unit orderbook threshold DOE's Liftoff report estimates microreactor manufacturers need to justify dedicated factory capacity — meaning a shared orderbook aggregating several buyers like Equinix could reach that threshold faster than any single buyer alone.

nuclear_aggregation.name: UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project (NuScale) — member subscription model
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: UAMPS aggregated ~27 municipal utility members' demand for a 6-module NuScale VOYGR plant via a member-subscription model governed by a Budget and Plan of Finance (BPF): members subscribed to a share of output and could withdraw and be reimbursed for most out-of-pocket costs if the project's $/MWh exceeded an agreed threshold. Continuation required roughly 80% subscription, an internally set viability threshold.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Target price was raised to $58/MWh in 2021 when the project was downsized to 6 modules; by 2023 it had risen to $89/MWh (a 53% increase) as estimated construction cost rose from $5.3B to $9.3B (75% increase). UAMPS and NuScale mutually terminated the project on Nov 8 2023, citing insufficient subscription to proceed; NuScale stock fell >30% same day.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Symmetric, not tiered: every member had the same opt-out right at the same price ceiling regardless of when they joined — there was no reward for early commitment and no penalty for waiting, so members had every incentive to wait and see rather than commit early, which is argued as a structural driver of the subscription shortfall.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: The clearest cautionary precedent for a microreactor orderbook: an opt-out-only pool with no early-mover benefit and no cost-overrun backstop beyond individual withdrawal rights collapsed once costs rose, because rational members simply exercised the opt-out rather than absorbing shared risk — the opposite of what a risk pool needs to do.

nuclear_aggregation.name: DOE $900M Gen III+ SMR solicitation (Tier 1/Tier 2)
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: DE-FOA-0003485 splits $900M into Tier 1 'First Mover Team Support' (up to $800M for up to two utility-led teams deploying initial Gen III+ SMR plants) and Tier 2 'Fast Follower Deployment Support' (~$100M for design, licensing, supply-chain, and site-prep gaps at additional projects). Funded via the 2021 IIJA and FY2024 Consolidated Appropriations Act.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Tier 1 awards of $800M announced Dec 2025 to Tennessee Valley Authority and Holtec Government Services (projects in Tennessee and Michigan).
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Explicitly tiered by order of entry: the first movers (Tier 1) receive the large award (~$800M for ≤2 teams) while fast followers (Tier 2) split a much smaller pool (~$100M) — first movers get a materially bigger government subsidy per project in exchange for bearing FOAK risk.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: A live, government-funded example of the 'first movers get the bigger benefit' design answer applied to nuclear at federal scale — directly analogous to a microreactor risk pool giving unit 1-n a larger subsidy/rebate than later entrants.

nuclear_aggregation.name: DOE Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP) 50/50 cost share
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Competitively awarded 50/50 public-private cost share in 2020: ~$2B in DOE funding to TerraPower's Natrium (sodium fast reactor) and ~$1.2B to X-energy's Xe-100 (with a TRISO fuel fabrication facility), with industry partners matching dollar-for-dollar. DOE commits $3.2B total over seven years subject to appropriations.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Both demonstration projects remain underway as of 2026 (TerraPower signed Hyundai as EPC for eight Natrium reactors, Aug 2026); these are single-project demonstrations, not multi-buyer orderbooks.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Not applicable — ARDP funds one FOAK project per design, not a sequence of buyers.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: Baseline government co-funding precedent both the NIA and EFI Foundation papers cite as necessary but insufficient on its own — it de-risks design/construction of the FIRST plant but does nothing to aggregate demand or share cost-overrun risk across a fleet, which is exactly the gap an orderbook + risk pool is meant to fill.

nuclear_aggregation.name: Nuclear Innovation Alliance — "Catalyzing Commitments to Advanced Nuclear Energy Projects" (June 2024)
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Based on 2023-24 Chatham House Rule workshops. Recommends: serial multi-project development to share FOAK costs across a design; offtakers sharing development/permitting/licensing costs in exchange for later compensation (offtake price adjustment or project-return participation); premium offtake pricing until the technology matures; and — 'the most impactful private-sector action' — offtakers making capital commitments as a completion-cost backstop in exchange for compensation and estimate-review rights. Publicly proposes a deductible ('an initial increment of increased costs') plus copayment ('a share of further increases') retained by the sponsor even after government backstop funding kicks in, to preserve cost-discipline incentives.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Policy proposal only, published as a working paper; explicitly cites DOE's 'committed orderbook of 5-10 deployments of a single reactor design' as the benchmark needed for commercial liftoff. Also notes potential offtakers (Google, Microsoft, Nucor) had already issued a joint 'Advanced Clean Electricity RFI' (March 2024) signaling advance-commitment interest.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Does not prescribe a first-vs-later price differential directly; instead recommends a deductible+copayment structure so sponsors of ANY vintage retain skin in the game on cost overruns, with government/backstop capital covering only the tail beyond that.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: Provides the clearest deductible/copayment vocabulary for designing a microreactor cost-overrun pool: sponsors bear a bounded first-loss layer, a shared/pooled layer covers 'normal' overruns, and an outside backstop (government or mutual insurer) covers only the extreme tail — directly transferable to a microreactor risk-pool design.

sources.label: Nuclear Innovation Alliance — full paper (PDF)
sources.quote: potential project participants have expressed strong interest in mechanisms to share the risk of cost overruns (e.g., sharing among an "order book")

nuclear_aggregation.name: EFI Foundation Cost Stabilization Facility (CSF) for an SMR orderbook
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Working paper (Oct 2023, updated as a Model Term Sheet Jan 2025) proposes: (1) a minimum-size orderbook (≥3 projects in the term-sheet version, illustrated at 10 units) of one SMR design; (2) an SPV holding company in which project sponsors (e.g., 5 utilities each building 2 units) own pro-rata undivided interests in every unit, enabling balance-sheet/rate-base treatment; (3) tiered cost sharing — sponsors fund the baseline budget (Tier 1) and a pooled IPD contingency fund (Tier 2) in full, and only once both are exhausted does a DOE Loan Programs Office backstop loan to the SPV (Tier 3) trigger automatically, illustrated at an 80% federal / 20% sponsor-equity split of the overrun; (4) flexible, deferred/graduated loan repayment tied to long-run project value.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Proposal only, not enacted; illustrative numbers: a 10-unit, $20B orderbook with a $5B (25%) contingency facility, FOAK unit at $2.45B declining to $1.79B for the 10th unit. Explicitly framed around 'the first mover disadvantage' as the core problem to solve.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: KEY DESIGN CHOICE — flat average pricing, not a declining schedule: "By aggregating several customers who will agree to pay an acceptable average price, the first/early disadvantage is erased... Instead of an inherent advantage in delaying being one of the last purchasers, in the orderbook concept, all the participants experience the same average cost based upon the total cost of all the units in the orderbook." All parties share FOAK downside AND later-unit savings equally via the pooled average.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: The single closest existing blueprint to the requested shared orderbook + shared risk pool for microreactors — SPV pooling, tiered contingency, government/mutual backstop, and an explicit, reasoned rejection of price discrimination by order position in favor of one blended average price precisely so nobody is incentivized to hang back and wait.

sources.quote: all the participants experience the same average cost based upon the total cost of all the units in the orderbook

nuclear_aggregation.name: DOE "Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear" — committed orderbook framework
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: DOE's flagship framework (March 2023, updated Sept 2024) defines three overlapping liftoff phases — committed orderbook, project delivery, industrialization — and states a committed orderbook of 5-10 units of one design (30-50 for microreactors specifically, since microreactor manufacturers need more units to justify factory capacity at their much smaller per-unit MW) is the first essential step. Distinguishes a 'buyers' consortium' (offtakers pool demand and agree to one average price for the whole set) from a 'builders' consortium' (asset owners spread early costs across the set). Directly invokes Boeing's 787 launch strategy as precedent: "Boeing did not try to sell one very expensive 787 loaded up with all the costs of designing the plane... Instead, Boeing sold 50 787s to their first customer, spreading early costs over multiple planes in a single order." Quantifies a bulk-order effect: "Bulk ordering over 10 reactors could lead to a ~15% cost reduction of the first unit compared to a single build without order book."
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: As of Sept 2024, zero signed contracts to construct new US nuclear reactors existed despite MOUs/LOIs; DOE's own $900M Gen III+ solicitation is its attempt to operationalize this framework. Report also documents that costs fell ~30% and key testing milestones ran 38-76% faster from Vogtle Unit 3 to Unit 4 (twin units, same site), and that a 4-unit AP1000 build is projected at ~$7,500/kW vs. ~$8,300/kW for a 2-unit build.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Gives two different answers depending on the mechanism layer. (1) For pooled buyer pricing itself: recommends one blended AVERAGE price across the whole orderbook, same logic as EFI — "Consortium approaches allow customers to all be 'one fifth' of the orderbook versus 'waiting to be fifth.'" (2) For government incentives layered on top: explicitly recommends FRONT-LOADING extra government benefit to early movers — "Tiered grants, starting at the highest dollar amount for the first reactor and decreasing with each subsequent deployment, could offer partial risk assurance and motivate customers to accelerate commitments... Ensuring that first-movers receive the best deal could induce customers to commit earlier," and similarly for offtake-certainty support: "such that each reactor ordered represents the best deal, the second the next-best, and so on."
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: The single most directly on-point primary source for this research question. It resolves the 'should early orders get a slightly higher benefit' question with a two-layer answer directly usable for microreactor design: the buyer pool itself should charge one flat average price (no internal price discrimination, to kill the incentive to wait), while any OUTSIDE subsidy or backstop layered on top of the pool should explicitly be richest for the earliest entrants and taper for later ones.

sources.label: DOE Loan Programs Office — Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear (Sept 2024 PDF)
sources.quote: Ensuring that first-movers receive the best deal could induce customers to commit earlier

precedents.name: GAVI Pneumococcal Advance Market Commitment (AMC)
precedents.mechanism: Five donor governments plus the Gates Foundation pledged $1.5B (pilot, 2009) to guarantee vaccine manufacturers a price. Manufacturers committed for 10 years to supply a share of 200M target doses/year at a long-term 'tail price' of $3.50/dose, and received an AMC top-up of an additional $3.50/dose (doubling revenue) on approximately the first 20% of doses supplied — the subsidized tranche was proportional to each manufacturer's supply commitment, funded from the shared $1.5B pool.
precedents.outcome: 161M doses procured through the AMC in 2019; 1.65B doses contracted through 2027 across 7 supply agreements; 3 vaccines developed, >150M children immunized, ~700,000 lives saved, 6-7.5M disease cases averted and 14-17M DALYs saved through 2015.
precedents.early_vs_late: Uniform subsidy, not tiered by order position: every qualifying manufacturer/dose in the subsidized 20% tranche received the same $3.50/dose top-up regardless of when it entered the AMC — the AMC pays the SAME price to all, with the subsidy defined by volume share not arrival order.
precedents.relevance: A working precedent for a flat, volume-proportional subsidy layer (not a first-mover premium) funded from a shared pool — an alternative design to the DOE Liftoff report's 'front-load the first mover' recommendation; useful as the counter-case in Part 4.

precedents.name: Frontier Climate advance market commitment (Stripe, Alphabet, Shopify, Meta, McKinsey)
precedents.mechanism: Launched April 2022 with a >$1B target (later raised to $1.8B via additional buyers including Google, Salesforce, H&M, Anthropic). Structured as two tracks: (1) low-volume 'prepurchase agreements' for early-stage suppliers piloting new technologies, and (2) 'offtake agreements' for growth-stage suppliers, promising to buy future delivered tons to help them secure scale-up financing. Frontier explicitly designs prices to be higher for earlier, riskier tons.
precedents.outcome: $1.8B total committed as of the most recent expansion; funded early deals including Charm Industrial (2023) and subsequent DAC and ocean/mineralization offtakes through 2025.
precedents.early_vs_late: Explicit, deliberate premium for EARLY suppliers/tons: "likely mean paying higher initial prices per ton to accelerate technologies that meet specific criteria" (permanence, cost trajectory, capacity). The design rationale is stated directly: pay more up front to send a demand signal and pull down the industry cost curve for everyone who buys later — the opposite of the DOE/EFI nuclear logic of one flat average price.
precedents.relevance: Direct real-world confirmation of the 'early buyers subsidize the market and pay MORE, not less, per unit' model — a third distinct answer (alongside GAVI's flat subsidy and aviation's early-discount model) to the 'who gets the better deal' design question for Part 4.

precedents.name: First Movers Coalition (World Economic Forum)
precedents.mechanism: A public-private coalition (WEF + US government) in which member companies make forward purchasing pledges for emerging low-carbon materials and fuels (green steel, aluminum, cement, shipping, aviation, CDR) years before commercial-scale supply exists, intended to be 'the world's largest private-sector demand signal.' Members commit to a defined % of their annual procurement volume in a target technology by a target year, rather than a single fixed contract.
precedents.outcome: 101 companies had pledged $19B in purchasing commitments by 2030 as of early-2026 reporting (some sources cite $16B+ at earlier count); FMC surfaces qualified suppliers to buyers and coordinates offtake terms to align with suppliers' capex milestones.
precedents.early_vs_late: Not price-differentiated by order position; FMC coordinates 'long duration offtakes, synchronized with suppliers' investment milestones' — the benefit to being an early pledger is influence over which suppliers/technologies get validated and qualified, not a lower price.
precedents.relevance: Shows demand aggregation can work as a pledged-percentage commitment across many buyers with no single binding master contract — a lighter-weight alternative to an SPV-style orderbook, useful if a microreactor buyers' club starts as soft percentage pledges before hardening into binding preorders.

precedents.name: Aircraft launch-customer economics (Boeing 787 / industry learning-curve pricing)
precedents.mechanism: Boeing launched the 787 program in April 2004 with All Nippon Airways as launch customer ordering 50 aircraft (list value ~$6B, actual price undisclosed but heavily discounted). Industry-standard aircraft learning-curve pricing has the manufacturer price early units below actual production cost (a loss-leader), recouping the deficit only once cumulative production volume pushes unit cost below price at a 'break-even point'; learning curves in aircraft manufacturing typically run 80-90% (each production doubling cuts labor input by 10-20%).
precedents.outcome: 787 program proceeded to full commercial scale; by 2011 first ANA revenue flight; program has since delivered well over 1,000 787s.
precedents.early_vs_late: EARLY/launch customers get the STEEPER discount, priced below the manufacturer's own cost, precisely because they are compensating the manufacturer for accepting first-mover technology and schedule risk on an unproven airframe — the opposite direction from GAVI's flat subsidy, and the opposite of a 'later buyers get it cheaper' intuition. The manufacturer, not other buyers, absorbs the early loss, betting on volume to earn it back.
precedents.relevance: The precedent DOE's own Liftoff report cites by name for nuclear orderbooks. Confirms that in a single-manufacturer, high-fixed-cost, standardized-product industry, the launch customer is compensated with the best price for bearing pioneer risk — directly supporting a design where a microreactor manufacturer (not the buyer pool) subsidizes early units, rather than later buyers cross-subsidizing early ones.

precedents.name: Operation Warp Speed advance purchase agreements
precedents.mechanism: US government funded six vaccine candidates through a mix of R&D funding, manufacturing-scaleup subsidies, and advance-purchase agreements (APAs) that let manufacturers build production capacity 'at risk' before trial results were known, so doses were ready immediately upon FDA authorization. Structure varied by company: some (Moderna, J&J, Sanofi/GSK, Merck/IAVI) got both R&D funding and purchase commitments; Pfizer/BioNTech took a pure APA ($1.95B for 100M doses) with no direct R&D funds.
precedents.outcome: OWS invested roughly $10-18B total to support late-stage development and manufacturing scale-up; individual APAs included $1.95B/100M doses (Pfizer), $1.6B (Novavax), $1.79B (Sanofi), $1B (J&J), $2.1B (Sanofi/GSK). Vaccines reached market in under a year, a fraction of the typical decade-long timeline.
precedents.early_vs_late: Not an orderbook among multiple buyer-members — it is a single buyer (US government) using APAs to shift financial and schedule risk off manufacturers, not a mechanism that differentiates price by which manufacturer/dose arrived first. No public early-vs-late price differentiation.
precedents.relevance: Precedent for 'pay for at-risk capacity before performance is proven,' relevant to funding factory tooling for a microreactor line ahead of a full orderbook being locked — but it is a single deep-pocketed buyer absorbing risk, not a shared multi-buyer risk pool, so it maps more to the DOE LPO/backstop-loan half of a microreactor mechanism than to the buyer-pool half.

precedents.name: DOE SunShot Initiative
precedents.category: technology cost-target program (R&D + soft-cost, not a block-buy)
precedents.mechanism: Launched Feb 2011 with a target to cut total solar costs 75% by 2020 (to ~$0.06/kWh utility-scale), pursued mainly through R&D funding and soft-cost reduction (permitting, financing, installation) rather than a government demand-aggregation purchase mechanism.
precedents.outcome: The utility-scale $0.06/kWh target was hit in 2017, three years early (down from ~$0.28/kWh in 2011); DOE then set a follow-on 'SunShot 2030' target of $0.03/kWh.
precedents.early_vs_late: Not applicable — SunShot did not aggregate buyer demand or allocate benefits by order position; it funded R&D and process/soft-cost improvements economy-wide.
precedents.relevance: Useful as a contrast case: a technology-cost-curve program can beat its target WITHOUT any buyer-side orderbook or risk pool at all, by attacking R&D and soft costs directly — a reminder that demand aggregation is one lever among several, and a microreactor program should not assume an orderbook alone will move the cost curve if manufacturing/soft-cost barriers dominate.

sources.label: DOE — SunShot Initiative overview
sources.quote: solar industry achieved SunShot's original 2020 cost target of $0.06 per kilowatt-hour for utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) solar power three years ahead of schedule

precedents.name: NYSERDA offshore wind block solicitations
precedents.mechanism: New York competitively solicits offshore wind capacity in sequential rounds; winning projects lock in a fixed 'strike price' for a 25-year contract term via NYSERDA, intended to give developers bankable long-term revenue certainty and to let the state compare/ratchet prices across successive rounds.
precedents.outcome: SURPRISE — the cost curve went the WRONG way in the most recent rounds: the 2023 solicitation's weighted-average strike price was $96.72/MWh (2023 real $) / $145.07/MWh nominal; the 2024 solicitation's weighted-average all-in cost was $150.15/MWh, 'on par with the latest market prices' — i.e., rising, not falling. Separately, developers holding ALREADY-AWARDED 2023 contracts petitioned in 2023 for price relief of 27-66% (avg. requested increase 48%, to $167.25/MWh) citing inflation and supply-chain cost escalation.
precedents.early_vs_late: No orderbook-style early/late differentiation by design — each solicitation round is priced independently at that round's market-clearing level. In practice this meant LATER rounds cost MORE, the opposite of a learning-curve decline, because global supply-chain and interest-rate inflation (2022-2024) outweighed any project-specific learning effect.
precedents.relevance: A direct, close-in-time cautionary counter-example to the 'sequential procurement rounds drive costs down' assumption embedded in nuclear-orderbook thinking (UAMPS drew the same lesson) — a microreactor risk pool needs a mechanism for macro cost inflation (materials, interest rates, labor) that is separate from and can overwhelm the learning-curve effect the orderbook is meant to capture.

precedents.name: Sematech semiconductor consortium
precedents.mechanism: 14 leading US semiconductor manufacturers formed Sematech in 1987 with US government support: DARPA/DoD provided $100M/year, matched by industry contributions, funding a roughly $240M annual budget (industry covering about half). Government matching funds were eliminated after 1996 per a Sematech board decision, after which the consortium broadened from a US-only to an international membership.
precedents.outcome: Economic analysis found Sematech membership caused participating firms to CUT their own private R&D spending by roughly $300M/year — about 3x the government subsidy amount — indicating the consortium mainly reduced costly duplicated R&D across members rather than adding net new spending.
precedents.early_vs_late: Not an orderbook/pricing mechanism at all — it pooled R&D cost and IP sharing among simultaneous member-competitors, not sequential buyers of a product; no early/late buyer distinction applies.
precedents.relevance: Relevant to the KNOWLEDGE-SHARING half of a microreactor consortium (not the orderbook or risk-pool half): shows a government-seeded, time-limited (government funding sunset after ~9 years) industry consortium can durably cut duplicated R&D costs even after public funding ends — informs how long DOE/public backstop support for a microreactor risk pool might need to run before the private sector can sustain it alone.

risk_pooling.name: NEIL (Nuclear Electric Insurance Limited)
risk_pooling.mechanism: Mutual insurer founded 1980 after Three Mile Island, owned by its member utilities (US, Belgian, Spanish companies), governed by a board drawn largely from member-company executives. Covers property damage, decontamination, extended-outage/business-interruption, and environmental-impairment liability for operating plants — up to $2.75B per site for property/decontamination. Separately runs a 'Member Nuclear Builders' Risk Program' for the CONSTRUCTION phase specifically, also up to $2.75B per occurrence, with sublimits for delay-in-startup and natural hazards; its sister organization ANI ran a Builders Risk Reinsurance Pool that reinsured construction of Vogtle Units 3 and 4.
risk_pooling.outcome: Financially strong as of 2024: assets >$5B, surplus >$4B, AM Best 'A (Excellent)' rating (June 2025) describing balance-sheet strength as 'strongest.' The construction-risk product is already being extended to new advanced-reactor builds.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not applicable — NEIL prices risk per plant/occurrence based on underwriting, not by a buyer's position in an orderbook.
risk_pooling.relevance: Directly answers the research question's NEIL angle: a NEIL-like mutual does NOT need to be invented for microreactor construction risk — NEIL already operates a builder's-risk product used on Vogtle and is structurally the kind of member-owned mutual that could be extended/scaled to a standardized-microreactor construction-overrun pool, though its existing product is a per-project insurance policy, not a cross-project cost-averaging orderbook mechanism.

risk_pooling.name: Price-Anderson Act two-tier liability pooling
risk_pooling.mechanism: Federal law (since 1957, repeatedly renewed) creating a two-tier system for THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY (not construction cost) from a nuclear incident: Tier 1 is commercial insurance each licensed site must carry, currently $500M per site, paid without the public having to prove negligence. Tier 2 is industry self-insurance: if damages exceed the $500M primary layer, ALL operating reactors nationwide (~92-94 units) are retroactively assessed a share, up to a capped deferred premium per reactor, administered by American Nuclear Insurers (ANI).
risk_pooling.outcome: Combined tiers currently provide on the order of $15.5B in total public compensation capacity per incident industry-wide; the Act has been renewed multiple times (most recently extended through 2025+ legislation) and is credited with keeping nuclear liability insurable at all, since no single private insurer would cover full nuclear-accident tail risk.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not applicable to order position — it pools risk across ALL currently operating reactors simultaneously, retroactively, regardless of each plant's age or when it joined the fleet; every reactor is assessed the same per-unit share when the secondary layer is triggered.
risk_pooling.relevance: The classic nuclear-industry template for 'pool small individual contributions to cover a tail risk too large for any single firm to insure alone' — directly transferable in STRUCTURE (not purpose) to a microreactor construction-cost-overrun pool: a first layer of dedicated/committed capital per project, and a second layer of retrospective, equally-assessed contributions from the whole fleet of microreactor buyers if the first layer is exhausted.

risk_pooling.name: UK Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model for Sizewell C
risk_pooling.category: consumer-funded construction cost-sharing (overrun risk shared with ratepayers)
risk_pooling.mechanism: Sizewell C is funded via the RAB model: consumers pay a levy on electricity bills DURING construction (not just after commissioning), giving the developer/investors a revenue stream and a regulated, lower cost of capital in exchange for accepting only limited government/consumer protection against cost overruns. As of Dec 2025 the RAB charge added 0.3p/kWh to UK domestic and business electricity unit rates specifically to fund Sizewell C construction.
risk_pooling.outcome: Government's own 2017 National Audit Office modeling found that IF the RAB model cuts the required investor rate of return from 9% to 6%, the resulting consumer saving would be equivalent to absorbing a 75-100% construction cost overrun for free — i.e., the financing-cost reduction from de-risking investors can be worth as much as the overrun itself. Critics counter that RAB functions as an 'open cheque book' for developers, since 'the taxpayer is taking an unknown and uncertain risk of cost overruns' and investors get guaranteed profits while consumers bear the overrun risk.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not an early/late buyer distinction — RAB shifts risk from investors to ALL current ratepayers collectively and continuously throughout construction, rather than differentiating by when any given consumer started paying into the scheme.
risk_pooling.relevance: A real, currently-live alternative risk-transfer design (payers-during-construction absorb overrun risk in exchange for a lower cost of capital that can outweigh the overrun) distinct from both an SPV-orderbook (EFI) and a mutual mirror-pool (NEIL/Price-Anderson) — relevant if a microreactor program considers a subscription/rate-base-like funding stream from committed off-takers rather than pure equity/debt.

risk_pooling.name: Vogtle Units 3 & 4 — who ate the cost overrun, and the Westinghouse fixed-price EPC lesson
risk_pooling.category: cost-overrun allocation case study / EPC contract-structure lesson
risk_pooling.mechanism: Original 2-unit budget ~$14B (2008-09), original completion target 2016; Westinghouse and CB&I Stone & Webster held a FIXED-PRICE EPC contract to jointly design AND construct — collapsing reactor-designer, constructor, and project-manager into one entity. That fixed-price contractor absorbed cost growth until it broke: Westinghouse filed for bankruptcy March 17, 2017, driven by the cost of performing under the fixed-price EPC. Owners (led by Southern Nuclear/Georgia Power) then had to take over direct project management themselves — a role they were unprepared for — hiring Bechtel as prime contractor and resetting the budget in 2017 to ~$26-27B, a figure the DOE Liftoff report notes was 'substantially closer to the final cost' than the original estimate.
risk_pooling.outcome: Final cost reached ~$32-35B (sources vary by what is included) against the original ~$14B — commonly cited as $35B final vs. ~$9B/~$14B original depending on scope counted, a >100% overrun. Westinghouse's collapse left $3.7B owed by Westinghouse absorbed into the settlement. Georgia's regulator (PSC) ultimately allowed Georgia Power to charge ratepayers $7.56B of the ~$10.2B Georgia Power's own share cost, while Southern Company/its shareholders absorbed the remaining ~$2.63B — average residential customers pay an extra ~$5-9/month. Independent monitors found Georgia Power had 'repeatedly provided materially inaccurate cost estimates,' and PSC rejected its own staff's recommendation to cancel the project.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not an early/late buyer question — Vogtle had a fixed 4-owner consortium (Georgia Power 45.7%, Oglethorpe Power 30%, Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia 22.7%, Dalton Utilities 1.6%) from the start; the cost allocation split that mattered was shareholder-vs-ratepayer, not first-mover-vs-later-mover.
risk_pooling.relevance: THE cautionary case for why a pure fixed-price EPC transfers too much risk onto one contractor to be viable at nuclear-scale complexity: the contractor (not the buyer pool) ate the overrun until it went bankrupt, which then forced an even messier, costlier owner-led rescue — arguing for a microreactor risk pool to spread overrun risk across MULTIPLE parties (owners + insurer/backstop + contractor, each within a bounded layer) rather than dumping it all on one fixed-price EPC counterparty. Vogtle Unit 4 was also ~30% cheaper and 20% more efficient than Unit 3 (same site, same owners) — the cleanest empirical twin-unit learning-curve datapoint in this research.

risk_pooling.name: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind (CVOW) tiered cost-overrun sharing
risk_pooling.mechanism: Virginia State Corporation Commission ruling (Dec 2022, docket PUR-2021-00142) on Dominion's 2.6 GW, 176-turbine CVOW project: if actual construction cost exceeds the initial $9.8B estimate, the overrun is split between Dominion (the company) and its customers on a SLIDING, TIERED schedule that shifts progressively more of the burden onto the company as the overrun grows — $9.8-10.3B: 100% customers/0% company; $10.3-11.3B: 50%/50%; $11.3-13.7B: 0% customers/100% company; above $13.7B: disposition determined by a future SCC proceeding, with the ruling noting Virginia's legislature is 'uniquely positioned to align general fund appropriations' if that threshold is reached.
risk_pooling.outcome: Regulatory precedent cited approvingly by the EFI Foundation's SMR cost-stabilization-facility paper as a model for a formal tiered risk schedule; construction was scheduled to begin in 2024.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not an early/late buyer mechanism — it's a single project with one customer base and one company, tiered by MAGNITUDE of overrun rather than by timing of commitment.
risk_pooling.relevance: A ready-made, regulator-approved template for the exact 'who pays how much of the overrun, in what order' schedule a microreactor risk pool needs: define bands of overrun severity and assign an escalating cost-share percentage to the backstop/insurer as each band is breached, rather than an all-or-nothing single trigger.

risk_pooling.name: ARC Act of 2026 — proposed federal nuclear cost-overrun backstop
risk_pooling.mechanism: Bipartisan bill (Sens. Jim Risch R-ID and Ruben Gallego D-AZ), reintroduced/updated Feb 2026 as the 'Accelerating Reliable Capacity (ARC) Act.' Would authorize up to $3.6B total to help offset cost overruns across three or more next-generation nuclear reactor projects; a qualifying project must have an expected cost of at least $2.5B to access up to $1.2B in cost-overrun protection per project; funded by repurposing existing IRA/bipartisan-infrastructure-law appropriations rather than new spending.
risk_pooling.outcome: Introduced/reintroduced as of Feb 2026; not yet enacted into law as of this research (status: bill text posted, sponsor press releases and trade-press coverage, no reported floor vote).
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Explicitly requires 'three or more' projects — i.e., federal backstop capital is only unlocked once a real multi-project orderbook exists, directly operationalizing the DOE Liftoff report's '5-10 unit orderbook' and EFI's '≥3 project' minimums into a funded backstop mechanism, though the bill text as summarized does not specify a first-mover-vs-later-mover split of the $3.6B across the qualifying projects.
risk_pooling.relevance: The most current (2025-2026) live legislative attempt to build exactly the kind of government backstop layer the EFI/NIA papers proposed conceptually — evidence the 'shared risk pool triggered only once a real orderbook exists' design pattern has bipartisan political traction right now, not just think-tank interest.

risk_pooling.name: Marsh/TerraPower Kemmerer Unit 1 — first commercial insurance placement for a US next-gen reactor
risk_pooling.category: 2025-2026 private insurance product for advanced-reactor construction
risk_pooling.mechanism: Insurance broker Marsh placed a construction-phase insurance program for TerraPower's Kemmerer Unit 1 (Natrium sodium-fast reactor, Wyoming) — described as 'the first time a next-generation U.S. nuclear plant has gained direct access to the commercial insurance marketplace.' The placement is backed by a mix of US, London, and Bermuda commercial insurers PLUS the traditional nuclear mutual pools (NEIL/ANI-type vehicles) and risk-retention groups, i.e., commercial capacity layered on top of the mutual pools rather than replacing them.
risk_pooling.outcome: Reported March 2026; specific coverage limits, deductibles, and premium were not disclosed in press coverage.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not disclosed — single-project placement, not a multi-buyer or multi-project pricing schedule.
risk_pooling.relevance: Shows the private insurance/reinsurance market is now willing to underwrite FOAK advanced-reactor construction risk directly (blending commercial capacity with the nuclear mutuals) rather than requiring 100% government backstop — a signal that a well-structured microreactor risk pool could plausibly attract layered commercial reinsurance once one or two demonstration units de-risk the design, rather than needing government capital indefinitely.

design_notes: What killed UAMPS: a symmetric opt-out (any member could withdraw at the same cost ceiling, joined early or late) gave zero reward for staying in and zero penalty for waiting, so when costs rose 53% (2021-23) members rationally exercised the exit right rather than absorb shared risk — a pool needs both a floor commitment AND a reason to stay, not just a right to leave.

There is no single universal answer to 'who gets the better deal, first movers or followers' — it depends on WHO is funding the subsidy. When the BUYER POOL itself sets price (EFI's nuclear SPV, DOE's buyers' consortium), the design converges on one flat AVERAGE price for every unit specifically so nobody is incentivized to wait ('all participants experience the same average cost'). When an OUTSIDE FUNDER subsidizes on top of that pool, DOE explicitly recommends front-loading the subsidy so first movers get the richest deal, decreasing for each later entrant. When the MANUFACTURER subsidizes (aircraft learning-curve pricing), the early/launch buyer gets the steepest discount, priced below the manufacturer's own cost, as compensation for schedule/technology risk. When a THIRD-PARTY donor pool subsidizes uniformly (GAVI AMC), every qualifying dose gets the identical subsidy regardless of arrival order. Frontier's AMC inverts the logic entirely and pays MORE per ton for earlier, riskier supply as a deliberate market-signal subsidy. A microreactor design needs to pick which of these four roles the 'early bonus' payer occupies before deciding the schedule.

Nearly every credible risk-sharing design converges on 2-3 discrete layers with a DIFFERENT payer per layer, never one blanket guarantee: Price-Anderson (per-site commercial insurance, then industry-wide retrospective assessment), EFI's CSF (sponsor pays baseline budget in full, then pooled IPD contingency, then an automatic government backstop loan once both are exhausted, illustrated at an 80% federal/20% sponsor split), CVOW (customers pay the first cost band, 50/50 the middle band, the company pays the top band), and NIA's proposal (sponsor deductible, then copayment, then government backstop). Build the microreactor pool as an explicit layered waterfall, not a single guarantee.

Orderbook size thresholds are technology-specific and NOT interchangeable: DOE's Liftoff report cites 5-10 committed units for SMRs/large reactors but 30-50 units specifically for microreactors, because microreactor factory capex has to be justified across far smaller per-unit MW (a 50-unit microreactor orderbook is still only ~500 MW total, achievable by a single industrial customer). A microreactor shared orderbook therefore needs proportionally MORE participating buyers than an SMR pool to reach the same manufacturing learning-curve trigger — do not import the 5-10 unit SMR number by analogy.

Fixed-price EPC contracts transfer too much risk to be viable at nuclear-construction complexity: Westinghouse's fixed-price Vogtle EPC contract (collapsing designer + constructor + project-manager into one entity) bankrupted the contractor in 2017 rather than protecting the owners, and the owner-led rescue that followed reset the budget from ~$14B to ~$26-32B+. DOE, NIA, and EFI all independently converge on Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) — shared incentive/contingency pools among owner, EPC, and designer — as the alternative, because it keeps everyone's incentives aligned toward completion rather than shifting the whole tail risk to one counterparty who then has an incentive to walk away.

Macro cost inflation can overwhelm learning-curve savings and defeat the 'sequential orders get cheaper' assumption entirely: NYSERDA's offshore wind strike prices ROSE across rounds (2023 weighted-avg ~$96.72-145.07/MWh -> 2024 ~$150.15/MWh, plus 27-66% renegotiation requests on already-awarded 2023 contracts), purely from 2022-24 interest-rate and supply-chain inflation, despite offshore wind being a maturing technology — the same macro shock (COVID-era inflation) that also broke UAMPS's nuclear subscription math. A microreactor risk pool needs an explicit, separate provision for economy-wide inflation/rate shocks, distinct from and layered outside the learning-curve/FOAK-risk provision, or a good design will still fail on a bad macro draw.

Credibility requires a BINDING commitment, not a signal of interest: DOE's Sept 2024 Liftoff report notes that despite multiple MOUs and letters of intent, zero signed contracts to construct new US nuclear reactors existed at that time — non-binding interest does not unlock supplier capex the way GAVI's legally-binding 10-year AMC commitment or Boeing's binding 50-aircraft launch order did. A microreactor orderbook needs enforceable preorders with real deposits (as Equinix–Radiant already demonstrates) rather than pledges, from day one.

Nuclear-specific risk-pooling infrastructure does not need to be invented from scratch — it already exists and is actively being extended to FOAK advanced reactors right now: NEIL/ANI's Member Nuclear Builders' Risk Program reinsured Vogtle 3&4's construction and was cited alongside commercial US/London/Bermuda insurers in Marsh's March 2026 placement for TerraPower's Kemmerer Unit 1 (called 'the first time a next-generation U.S. nuclear plant has gained direct access to the commercial insurance marketplace'), and the bipartisan ARC Act (introduced/reintroduced Feb 2026) would add a federal $3.6B backstop explicitly gated on 'three or more' qualifying projects. A microreactor pool's job is to adapt these existing vehicles to many more, much smaller, more standardized units — not to build parallel infrastructure.

Demand-pooling, knowledge-sharing, and risk-sharing are inseparable in every credible framework, and addressing only one is explicitly called out as insufficient: DOE's Liftoff report and EFI's CSF paper both structure their proposals around exactly these three 'interlocking elements.' Sematech is instructive on the DURATION question — its government matching funds sunset after ~9 years (1987-96), yet economic analysis found participating firms permanently cut ~3x the subsidy amount in duplicated private R&D — suggesting a microreactor consortium's government/backstop capital may only need to be transitional (until enough standardized units are built to de-risk the design) rather than a permanent subsidy.

Government cost-share programs consistently price the FIRST mover's subsidy larger than later movers' in DOE's own recent programs, not just in proposals: the $900M Gen III+ SMR solicitation splits $800M across ≤2 'First Mover' teams (Tier 1) versus only ~$100M shared among all 'Fast Follower' teams (Tier 2) — a roughly 8x-per-project difference in favor of going first. This is a live, already-funded (Dec 2025 awards to TVA and Holtec) precedent for the 'earlier orders get a materially bigger benefit' design, distinct from and complementary to a flat-average-price buyer pool sitting underneath it.
